Uruguay’s Electricity Grid Faces Disruption Amid River Blockade

MONTEVIDEO – Electric utilities in Uruguay are facing mounting challenges after a blockade was imposed yesterday on the Río Negro hydroelectric complex, a critical site for the country’s power generation. The blockade, currently enforced by a coalition of regional governments citing a dispute over water rights and cross-border energy exports, has brought significant uncertainty to the electricity sector.

The Río Negro complex, operated by Energía Oriental S.A., accounts for nearly 35% of Uruguay’s total electricity supply, making it a vital component of the national grid. Since the blockade began, access roads and river transport to the facility have been sealed, preventing the delivery of essential maintenance equipment and restricting the movement of technical staff.

“We are doing everything possible to keep generation stable, but the situation is extremely tense,” said Energía Oriental’s chief operations officer, Lucía Fernández, during a press briefing in Montevideo. “Our teams are on site and working under significant logistical constraints. If the blockade continues, we could see generation capacity decrease within days.”

Preliminary estimates from the Uruguayan Electric Utilities Association suggest that electricity output from the Río Negro plant has already dropped by 12% since early this morning. Grid operators are now forced to rely more heavily on backup thermal power plants and energy imports from neighboring countries, which comes at a higher cost and places added strain on the system.

“This blockade poses a serious risk to our ability to provide stable electricity, especially during peak hours,” warned association president Mario Vázquez. “If this continues into next week, we may have to consider rolling blackouts in some regions.”

The National Electric Workers Union has voiced concerns about worker safety and potential job losses if the situation is not resolved soon. “Our members are deeply worried—not only about their own safety, but about the impact on Uruguayan families and businesses,” said union representative Carla Méndez.

Government officials have confirmed ongoing negotiations to resolve the dispute, but have not provided a timeline for when the blockade might be lifted. “Our priority is to restore full access to the Río Negro complex and ensure a reliable electricity supply for all Uruguayans,” said Energy Minister Rafael Silva.

Uruguay’s electric utilities industry is now bracing for further uncertainty as talks continue and the blockade remains in effect. The coming days are expected to be critical for the stability of the national electricity grid.
